headline: High-risk shared-network pair: broad egress, MCP/tooling, and shared mutable web sessions create dangerous leakage and cascading-error pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LightAgent can use MCP and stdin/stdout, while open-webui exposes MCP, plugins, and tool servers. That creates a plausible instruction-injection bridge if one agent forwards the other’s content through shared channels. The pathway is not proven by direct pair evidence, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF LightAgent forwards open-webui-generated text into MCP/tool prompts without provenance checks
IF open-webui ingests LightAgent outputs as trusted instructions via plugins or tool calls
mitigations: Disable MCP between the two agents for the first run
Add a strict allowlist for tool-call arguments
Insert a provenance tag on all inter-agent messages
Review one sample exchange for prompt-like content before enabling automation

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents handle secrets and broad user data; open-webui can read local files and mounted volumes, and LightAgent handles API keys and workflow state. With broad network egress on both sides, a shared workspace or forwarded context can leak sensitive data to external services. The pairwise interaction is inferred, but the blast radius is clearly sensitive.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mounted data volume or shared workspace
IF either agent forwards file contents or conversation context to external APIs
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different workspaces
Remove secrets from shared files before enabling either agent
Turn on offline mode for open-webui where possible
Block outbound traffic except to approved endpoints
Rotate any API keys exposed in shared artifacts

C_capability_conflict.rationale: LightAgent supports multiple instances and subprocesses, and open-webui supports persistent shared sessions with Redis-backed shared state plus mounted files. If both write to the same directory or session-backed resource, concurrent mutation can corrupt state or overwrite artifacts. Because no locking is documented here, uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same mounted directory or shared session store
IF concurrent runs are enabled without external locking
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate writable directory
Disable concurrent runs during shared-resource access
Use file-level locks or a single-writer policy
Snapshot shared state before running both agents

D_cascading_error.rationale: open-webui is designed around plugins, tools, and function calling, so it may act on LightAgent outputs; LightAgent also emits tool results and workflow state that can be treated as authoritative. Without an explicit verification step, one agent’s errors can cascade into the other’s actions or rendered outputs. The interaction is plausible in default setups, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF open-webui consumes LightAgent outputs as tool inputs or final answers
IF no verification or human review step is inserted between them
mitigations: Require a verification step before any action-taking tool call
Mark LightAgent outputs as untrusted in open-webui
Limit open-webui to read-only rendering for the first deployment
Log and diff one end-to-end run before enabling automation

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents touch persistent memory and files, but open-webui additionally exposes Google Drive, OneDrive/SharePoint, and analytics surfaces while LightAgent handles user conversations and long-term memory. That creates a plausible retention/residency mismatch if the same data class is routed through both systems. No direct residency policy conflict is documented, so medium fits.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through open-webui connectors or analytics
IF LightAgent memory is synchronized into open-webui persistence without matching retention rules
mitigations: Classify data before routing it between agents
Disable analytics for regulated workloads
Set matching retention windows on both systems
Avoid syncing long-term memory across the pair
